BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
May 6, 20266:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen,
Selectman Peter Gagyi, Selectman Sandy Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin, Excused, Jenn Miskovic Account Clerk (Covering)
1.
II.
III.
Call to Order:
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00 PM.
Citizens Comment
Sue Whitbeck was in and advised the Board that she would like to nominate Ryan
O'Hora as Librarian of the year and that she was wondering if the Board would write
a letter of Support. The Board had no issue with the request and the Chair would draft
something to be submitted.
Sharon Morris proposed moving the farmers market/craft fair to the Pembroke Park at
the top of Broadway for a trial run. If it works out well then she would be back to
make it a permanent location. This would run from June through the end of August
but not during Old Home Day.
Motion by Selectman Goulet to authorize the farmers market to take play on May 16"
at Pembroke Park, seconded by Selectman Christiansen. Motion passed 5-0
Scheduled Meetings:
Matt Petersons Suncook Little League - Waiving of Fees
Matt was in to request that the Board waived the league fees for Little League for the
season.
Matt stated that he worked out with the Recreation Director the use of the fields by
filling out all the necessary forms.
As part of this request Little League will continue to mow and maintain the major and
point fields as well as minimal maintenance.
Selectman Goulet commented that she is ok with the request for now but going
forward she felt that the Board really needed to look at this. The recreation
department makes its money off the play camp program.

With the discussion taking place about upgrading the middle field there is concern
because that was an old landfill.
The $450 is a lot for the small department.
Chairman Yeaton felt that going forward this should be a consideration of the
Recreation Commission first and then it's brought to the Selectmen.
Jenn reminded Matt that they needed to communicate with the Town better with
regards to the electricity shut off. Last year there was no communication and the
Town paid the bill from October on.
Motion by Selectman Goulet to waive the Little League fees of $450 due to the
expenses that they pay for field maintenance, seconded by Selectman Christiansen.
Motion passed 5-0.
Chief Paulsen Forest Fire Warden and Federal forms
Chief Paulsen was in to request that the Board re-appoint the listing of candidates for Forest
Fire Warden and to approve the necessary paperwork to retain the Federal surplus equipment.
The appointees are Josh Ginn, Brian Lemoine, Tyrel Lemoine, Rob Farley and Chester
Martel.
Motion to approve the forest fire warden appointments and the federal excess property
cooperative agreements, seconded by Selectman Christiansen. Motion passed 5-0.
DPW Crack Sealing Bids
Motion by Selectman Goulet to approve the crack sealing bids to sealcoating Inc, seconded
by Selectman Gagyi. Motion passed 5-0.
Sgt. Pihl on behalf of the Central NH Special Operations Unit
Scott was in to walk the Board through the grant process that will allow the Town to purchase
on behalf of the CNHSOU certain equipment and the Town will receive reimbursement.
Because the dollar amount is over $10,000 he is here before the Board. There will be some
minor changes to the items purchased.
Chairman Yeaton opened the public hearing at 6:35 PM.
The Public Hearing was closed at 6:36 PM.
Motion by Selectman Goulet to waive the sealed bids requirements and to approve the gas
mask purchase from Atlantic tactical for the sum of $25, 144.20, seconded by Selectman
Christiansen. Motion passed 5-0.

IV.
Chief Shea Cruiser purchase
Chief Shea explained that when she submitted the information, she did not have at the time
the cost to outfit the vehicle. That information is now available. The vehicle that will be
cycled out to another department will be the Chevy Tahoe.
We would like to replace this with a Ford 150 pick-up truck.
We obtained three quotes. Grappone Ford in Bow came in at the lowest so I am asking the
Board approve the quote with them in the amount not to exceed $39,000.
Selectman Goulet questioned why Ford? Chief Shea explained that Ford is the only one who
provides a Police package.
Selectman Gagyi asked if the F150 would be able to access the range roads like the Tahoe
currently does. Chief Shea responded yes.
Selectman Christiansen asked the Chief if there was money in the budget for this and she
responded yes.
The second part of this that I gave you tonight is the outfitting of the vehicle. Of the three
quotes Global Public Safety came is significantly less than the others.
Selectman Miller questioned the Chief as to the difference between the quotes. Chief
explained they were all provided the specs.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to waive the bid requirements and to authorize the Chief to
proceed with purchasing a 2026 Ford F150 Police responder 4x4x super crew from Grappone
Ford in the amount not to exceed $49,000, seconded by Selectman Miller. Motion passed 5-0.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to waive the sealed bid requirement and to award the bid
for equipment to Global Public Safety with a sum not to exceed $16,000. Motion passed 5-0.
Old Business:
Tax Deeds
The Board reviewed the 2023 Tax Deeds. The Board decided to wait for David to
return because they had some procedural questions.
Tax Deed Waivers
Selectmen Miller had questions on the property that was in probate.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to issue tax deed waivers on the following
properties; VE-15-1, 266-27-2, VW-114-1, VE179-2, and VE-179-1, seconded by
Selectman Gagyi. Motion passed 5-0.

a. 2026 Road Projects Update
a. Robinson Road. The base of 2.5 inches has been put down. The road has been
ditched, trim has been started but needs to be completed and the shoulders have been
built and stabilized. Fourth Range Road is waiting for under drainage which goes from
Fifth Range Road about 700 feet on the Church Road side.
Members made comments regarding side roads. CNHRP plans do not include the side
roads which also need to be addressed to account for any additional costs needed to take
care of those areas.
Manhole issues on Route 3 need to be fixed. VJ walked Rt. 3 with DOT representative to
address cover adjustments. DOT has marked those which need to be fixed and they will
take care of.
4. Any Old Business:
5. New Business:
a. TRC Plans
b. Discuss Roads Rules and Regulations
a. Adam mentioned from a conversation with J that not much new on the Smith
Avenue plan. They are adding fence line but are not touching road drains.
b. Jason Menard had brought up to Board of Selectmen the Rules and Regulations
the Roads Committee currently has to work with and suggested that a
subcommittee be formed to review the rules. The Roads Committee had decided
at the last meeting that a subcommittee was not necessary but that they would
review. Since the rules and regulations are also a part of Planning Board
1

requirements, and the Select board has final say in projects brought before them,
it is very important that all are aware of those rules. There have been instances
where one builder has to follow those rules and another is granted permission to
proceed without adhering to the same set of rules. There needs to be consistency
in approving projects. The Board of Selectmen has final say on projects and it
seems that if a rule exists it either needs to be enforced or removed. If it is going
to be over ridden by the Select board, perhaps it should be removed from the
regulations. In any event all boards need to be in agreement over which rules will
apply. Sandy will bring this matter us at the next Select board meeting.
Selectmen need to be more on board with this situation. Planning board says one
thing and Select board says another Range Road development needs to be handled
better. Surveying needs to be done as actual location of property lines are not
currently marked. The Road Committee decided to Table the Roads Rules &
Regulations until the next meeting.

TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
January 7, 2026, at 6:00 PM

James Colorusso - 477 Fourth Range Road
James Colorusso, 477 Fourth Range Road, was present to discuss the waiver of the sprinkler
system requirement as previously discussed on December 17, 2025. Chairman Yeaton stated that
Mr. Calorusso would like the current policy waived which requires a sprinkler system for
driveways longer than 200 feet in length. Mr. Calorusso plans to build a single-family home at
477 Fourth Range Road. Chairman Yeaton added that the Selectboard has sought legal
consultation which has advised the Selectboard that there is no liability to the Town if they grant
such waiver,
Chief Paulsen, Pembroke Fire Chief, was present to discuss the matter. He clarified that the
ordinance states that "the water supply requirement can be met by using a municipal water
supply, cisterns, or sprinkler systems." He continued that often, sprinkler systems are the most
cost-effective solution, but that the Fire Department is not mandating sprinklers.
Chairman Yeaton expressed confusion if there is not a mandate in place.
Town Administrator David Jodoin explained that the ordinance was provided to legal counsel.
Legal counsel was asked if the ordinance is still valid and if such a waiver was granted, if there
would be any liability to the Town. She reviewed the ordinance in its entirety and explained that
in the State of New Hampshire, it is illegal to require sprinkler systems in single-family homes,
which she has explained to previous fire chiefs. She continued that the Selectboard much grant
the waiver, and that the requirement should be repealed as it cannot be enforced. She confirmed
that there is no liability to the Town. She also provided citations to the applicable state statutes
that she used to form this opinion. These statutes referenced were as follows: RSA 153:5 III,
RSA 153:10A III, RSA 155A:10-6 and RSA 674:36-6.

Selectman Miller asked David to repeat the reference to RSA 674:36-6. David repeated that the
statute states that "The planning board shall not require, ol adopt any regulation requiring, the
installation of a fire suppression sprinkler system in proposed one- or 2-family residences as a
condition of approval for a local permit. Nothing in this paragraph shall prohibit a duly adopted
regulation mandating a cistern, dry hydrant, fire pond, or other credible water source other than a
fire suppression sprinkler system." The Selectboard and David agreed that this is in reference to
the Planning Board.
Selectman Miller asked about Chapter 82 (Fire Prevention) or the Town Ordinance. David
clarified that this was updated by the Selectboard in November of 2019.
Selectmen Miller expressed that it was unfortunate that the discussion is about sprinklers when
this is really in reference to water supply. He added that he views the responsibility and
accountability being the homeowners, and if there is no liability on the Town, he would see it as
a homeowner decision and support granting a waiver.
Selectman Frederickson spoke about the language of Chapter 82 requiring use of a municipal
water supply, cisterns or sprinkler systems. He went on to state that the language does not
mandate any one of the three. Chief Paulsen pointed out the word "must" which would require
that one of the three is required under certain circumstances and a driveway that is more that 200
feet in length would qualify for this requirement.
David noted that the state statute references a "credible water source", which could include a fire
pond, dry hydrant or cistern.
Chief Paulsen added that it also references the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA)
Standards for Rural and Suburban Fire Fighting. Assistant Chief Farley added that this is also
included in the State Fire Code.
Selectman Frederickson asked Chief Paulsen what changes with the differential in driveway
length. For example, he asked what the difference would be between a driveway that was 199
feet and over 200 feet. Chief Paulsen responded that it takes more personnel, more time to get in.
He noted that when the ordinance was put in place, an exercise was done to see what a
reasonable distance would be for a crew of six to pull larger diameter handlines down the
driveway to begin suppression on the fire.
Selectman Christiansen reiterated that legal counsel has stated that the Town would not be liable
and that the sprinkler piece of this ordinance needs to be repealed. He recommended the Fire
Department and legal counsel meet to come to an agreement on how to proceed.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to grant the waiver from Chapter 82 Fire Prevention for Mr.
Colorusso at 477 Fourth Range Road. Selectman Miller seconded the motion. Motion passed 5-0.
David requested that Mr. Colorusso sign a waiver from the 200-foot requirement to be filed at
the Registry of Deeds. This would follow the property even after transfer of ownership. Mr.
Colorusso agreed to the request.

Selectman Christiansen suggested a motion be made to that effect.
Selectman Goulet made a motion to request a waiver for Mr. Colorusso at 477 Fourth Range
Road for the non-installation of a fire suppression systems. Selectman Frederickson seconded the
motion. Motion passed 5-0.
David stated that he would have something drafted for Mr. Colorusso and the Selectboard to sign
and then David would have it recorded at the Registry of Deeds.
Selectman Christiansen requested legal and the Fire Chief and Assistant Chief work on
something clearer and more concise regarding this ordinance.

She stated that there are currently three projects proposed in 2026, 2028 and 2030. She added

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
February 18, 2026, at 6:00 PM
Present: Selectman Matt Miller, Selectman Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman
Sandy Goulet, Selectman Rick Frederickson
Absent: None
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
I.
Call to Order:
II.
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00 pm.
Citizen Comment:
None
III.
Scheduled Meetings:
Rob Azevedo/Jacques Despres - Yearly Dump Fee
Selectman Yeaton invited Rob Azevedo, 250 Pembroke Street, and Jacques Despres, 128 Main
Street.
Mr. Azevedo requested that the Board approve payment for use of the transfer station on a
quarterly basis as opposed to on a yearly basis. He also requested a review of the fee amount. He
noted that he is not dumping two yards per week and was unsure at this time of what the fee
should be.
Mr. Despres agreed that the fee was a bit high for them and echoed the request for a quarterly
payment structure.
VJ Ranfos, Public Works Director, explained that they were then supposed to pay a yearly fee of
$1,800. There was some discussion about actual usage trends.
After review of the current pricing structure by VJ, Selectman Goulet expressed concern based
on the amount being charged. She noted that the town is not making any money and is not
including any administrative fees in the amount they are charging.
It was explained that the reason that this came about was that VJ noticed that these two
businesses were using the transfer station for business trash disposal. Mr. Azevedo expressed
concern that there are various contractors and possible others using it for business purposes, but
that they are the only two businesses being charged a commercial fee. Selectman Christiansen
noted that those contractors are paying for the service.

Selectman Goulet mentioned that this was presented originally as a safety issue with getting a
truck to pick up a dumpster behind the businesses, specifically Mr. Despres' business. There was
further discussion on the safety issue.
Selectman Frederickson stated that the Board of Selectman had agreed to this arrangement based
on safety issues presented by the businesses. He also stated that the agreement was that the fee
would be paid at the beginning of the year and that the cost may be adjusted depending on usage
after the originally agreed period.
Selectman Miller noted that there are two separate issues being discussed. The first, regarding
the fee for commercial dumping at the transfer station, was part of the original approval. The
second was the fee structure, yearly versus the request for a quarterly structure.
Selectman Goulet suggested, that if the payment structure is changed to quarterly, that the
amount is increased to due increased administrative costs. She also suggested implementing a
late fee.
Selectman Christiansen mentioned that there may be an opportunity to adjust fees based on
usage. He also stated that he would be okay with a quarterly fee structure but agreed that it
should be at a slightly higher rate.
Selectman Frederickson expressed concerns with changes to the agreement being requested
before it even began.
Selectman Yeaton appreciated both businesses for doing business in Pembroke. She stated that
Public Works does not have a sophisticated invoicing or billing system, which would be
expensive to obtain. She expressed concern with the burden that a quarterly payment system may
cause for town employees.
David Jodoin, Town Administrator, suggested tracking and billing by usage in the future. He
stated that if VJ, can provide usage details to Town Hall, they can bill the businesses using their
invoicing system.
Selectman Yeaton expressed that her concern is the effort required to execute the suggestion. She
wanted to understand the effort required for implementation of a quarterly billing system.
Selectman Frederickson spoke about Alex tracking the usage and Mr. Azevedo stated that he
asked him to start tracking it.
Selectman Yeaton stated that Public Works is not a business and noted that they are not making
money from the agreement. Mr. Despres argued that his employees still need to bring the trash to
the dump and that is a task for them as well. He also stated that some of the trash is from his
personal residence.

Selectman Frederickson noted that this was done for the convenience of the businesses and to
alleviate the safety issue of a dumpster being at the business. The price was set based on the fees
the businesses were paying previously to have a dumpster.
Selectman Goulet stated that she didn't like the idea of billing based on usage or billing after the
fact. She didn't feel that the effort to track usage would be worth it. Selectman Yeaton agreed
citing the added work and cost of administration and emphasized that Public Works is busy as it
is.
Selectman Yeaton asked the business owners what their ideal solution would be. Mr. Azevedo
stated that he feels that $1,200 per year or two payments of $600 per year would be fair.
Selectman Goulet suggested a fee of $1,500 broken up quarterly as a compromise. She also
wanted to ensure that the cost to the town is covered.
VJ stated that there is both trash and recycling that is separated. He added that the fee was
determined based on the dumpster size the businesses were using previously as opposed to actual
usage.
There was discussion on Selectman Goulet's suggestion for $1,500 per year paid in four $375
payments. Both Mr. Azevedo and Mr. Despres stated that they would agree with this fee and
structure.
Selectman Goulet noted that this would be subject to change. It was decided that the fee would
be reviewed every fall when the new Casella rates come out and updates would be made to the
ordinance for the following year.
VJ stated that he thought this was a good compromise.
Selectman Goulet suggested that late fees be discussed at a future date. The Board decided that
they would revisit after the year is over and J agreed to this.
Selectman Goulet suggested that she would prefer tracking from Public Works. She also stated
that she would like this billed prior to usage and David stated that he could implement an invoice
process.
Selectman Christiansen stated that the public hearing on the change to the ordinance would need
to be put on the agenda for next meeting.
VJ clarified that the dollar amount is not listed in the ordinance, and it simply states that it is
determined by the Director of Public Works. No public hearing would be necessary.
It was determined that the next review of the fee would be in the fall. A late fee structure would
be discussed at the next meeting.

Carolyn Cronin updated the subcommittee since the last time they met at the public forum
in November. She explained that Stephanie, the Planning Board rep, resigned from the
Planning Board, so Bob Bourque was appointed to replace her. The public forum was in
mid-November, the comment period was open until mid-December and then the holidays
happened, and since then Central NH Regional Planning Commission (CHRPC) have
been working on the bulk of the draft report. She had typed up all the public comments
from the forum and emails. She and CHRPC went back and forth on the report. She
included information about how the public forum operated and the subcommittee's efforts
to plan it. A lot of the report is public comments and information from the PowerPoint
presentation that was previously put together.
Carolyn Cronin explained that there are two tasks left for the subcommittee: finalize the
report and suggest recommendations based on the facts and on the public feedback
collected. The recommendations will be for the Select Board, Planning Board,
Conservation Commission, and other committees that have control over zoning
amendments, master plans, town policies, budgeting decisions, etc. to inform town policies
and regulations, because that is the scope of the subcommittee. The subcommittee's
charge is to decide how you want to process and package the feedback and integrate it
into recommendations.
Staff put together a first stab at feedback analysis and recommendations. Matt Miller also
put together a document with his feedback analysis. He also shared his edits and
comments on the draft report.
Matt Miller explained his suggestions for the report. He recommended the following:

alignment is the feature that intends to be highlighted.
• The document raises a few different types of questions about range roads. Some
questions were not addressed, depending what the town decides (traffic, utilities,
etc.)
Matt Monahan agreed that those are good questions for development, generally. He added
that the question might be how those factors are influenced by range roads compared to
other types of roads.
Matt Miller wanted to find a way to call out valid concerns that are raised by the report,
while also acknowledging that those solutions are outside of the scope of the study.
Carolyn Cronin suggested that those types of thoughts would be best suited for the
recommendation section as items that need further examination in relation to a town policy
or when applications to develop are brought forth.
The subcommittee moved on to discussing the public feedback and how to analyze and
present it.
Carolyn Cronin suggested there are a few ways to present the feedback. There could be
summaries for each Vision. She also looked at all the feedback and presented general
themes that came up as frequently mentioned. The challenge is that the data is qualitative,
not quantitative. She said that even comments that were "in favor" or "not in favor" of
certain scenarios were with caveats or concerns. She cautioned that they had to be careful
not to misrepresent the feedback as black and white.
Matt Miller found that for most of the scenarios there was a mixture of feedbacks, except
for Vision 3: Town Forest and Recreation Trails, which had consistent feedback of people
in favor of it.
Bob Bourque suggested both summarizing each scenario's comments and also including
the original comments for anyone to read. It was agreed that the original comments would
be included as an appendix to the report.
Chuck Schmidt explained that he volunteered with one of the master plans years ago. At
that time, the town indicated that they wanted to keep the middle of the town and range
roads as recreation. The philosophy hasn't changed even as new people come into town.

report.

discussed this and agreed that updating the current standards/regulations and

Ryan explained that since the last meeting he was asked to come back with some
different ideas since the Board did not want a six foot stockade fence in front of the
Library. He commented that Trustee Sue Whitbeck was unable to attend tonight.

The draft plan that you have before you is what Sue and I have come up with. We
agreed that we wanted to keep the dialog open with the Board so that you knew what
we were considering so everyone was on the same page.
Selectman Goulet asked the Director for clarification as to why he felt that they
needed fencing. Ryan explained that the Trustees had been looking at fencing for a
variety of reasons. Since we do the children's and adult programs outside at times we
were looking for some confined space for safety reasons instead of holding the
programs in the parking lot.
The Library received a $10,000 donation from a patron who passed away to use
towards a fence for the programs.
Selectman Goulet asked where the fencing would go. Ryan explained that it would go
in the front and attach to the current fencing that is on the driveway exit.
Ryan discussed the different types of fencing that would look good in the front. The
trustees met today and we had three different quotes and the Trustees decided to go
with American Fence in Hooksett which would be a spaced picket 5 feet high.
Part of the Trustees ask is to get approval from the Board to proceed with this style or
if the Board had a request for a different type. Ryan also questioned future
maintenance and upkeep.
Selectman Goulet stated that from reading the document it looked like the entire
$10,000 cover the cost. Ryan agreed that it did.
Selectman Miller stated that the last time Ryan was in the Board talked about
different types of plans that would accomplish the same things with boundaries such

Ryan responded to Selectmen Miller that he felt that the last discussion with the

Chairman Yeaton stated that the Board was looking at alternatives to a solid fence
regardless of the height.

Charrette discussion.

Selectman Gagyi asked about the square footage of the space.
Chairman Yeaton questioned if the Trustees looked at other options or was it just a
fence.

fence.

Ryan responded that the other side of the building is a sloped drop-off.

MEETING MINUTES
June 8, 2026
In attendance: Ammy Heiser (Co-Chair), Erin Insley (Co-Chair), Carol Bertsimas (Vice Chair), Brian
Mrazik (Secretary), Ayn Whytemare, Wendy Weisiger, Robert Bourque (PB Rep), Karen Yeaton (BOS

Stephen Richard, citizen

Call to Order: Meeting called to order at 7:03 PM.
Planning Board Applications: None
NDES Letters and Applications: None
Zoning Board Applications: None
City of Concord Planning and Conservation Coordination: Kearsten O'Brien, Concord City Planner,
and Kristine Tardiff, Chair Concord Conservation Commission met with the CC to discuss and
coordinate on issues of common interest and concern. Concord has over 800 acres of conservation area
and 80 miles of trails. Like Pembroke, Concord has realized a significant increase in public use of open
space since the COVID epidemic. In some cases, heavy use has had adverse environmental impacts on
conservation areas. To meet the greater needs for management of these properties, Concord has created
a Trails Subcommittee and has established a part-time Trail Steward position. The Trail Steward
conducts monthly educational hikes and conducts monitoring of the conservation areas. To help mitigate
adverse impacts Concord has also established a relationship with the New England Mountain Bike
Association to identify potential biking trails and promote responsible use of trails. Pembroke and
Concord share many objectives, including: updating zoning and wetland ordinances, the identification
and management of open space development projects and the management of open space in open-space
developments, invasive species management in conservation areas, and homeless encampments in open-
space areas. Concord and Pembroke need to work together on initiatives such as the rail trail and
protection of the Soucook River aquifer. The creation of a local association of conservation
commissions in the Concord area was discussed as an opportunity to foster greater communication and
coordination between the Towns.
Merrimack River Conservation Area Rail & Powerline Easements: Stephen Richard addressed the
CC regarding vehicular access to a portion of lot 565-52, along the Merrimack River, that he and his
family have actively farmed for generations. The only remaining access to this piece is from Bow Lane,
through the Eversource right-of-way along the old railroad bed. Several years ago, the Town acquired
conservation land along the river from the Whittemore family, that includes this right-of-way. Richard is
concerned that if the Town agrees to the conversion of the old railroad bed to the proposed rail trail, he
will lose access to the farmland for his farming equipment. Similar problems are occurring in other parts
of the State where heavy equipment crossings are being restricted on rail trails. The CC is not familiar
with the legal details of the historical rail and power easements associated with the property and how
this may impact future transportation use. Bob suggested that Richard contact Eversource to discuss the

possibility of a joint-use agreement for their access road. Wendy suggested that Richard obtain legal
advice as to whether he may have a prescriptive easement as a result of his long-term use of the
accessway. He was provided with a contact at Eversource and the name of the legal firm that did the title
work for the conservation area acquisition. The CC will try to obtain more information on the easements
and what is permitted under them. Ammy will contact Craig Tufts regarding how establishment of the
rail trail could impact farm equipment access.
Potential Acquisitions:
1. Gelinas Farm. The CC met again with representatives of FRCT and the owners of the Gelinas Farm
to follow-up on questions raised at our last meeting regarding any conditions for the use of the Town
Conservation Fund to pay the cost of the initial appraisal that is needed for the grant application. The CC
had previously voted to commit the funding without conditions, but some members were concerned that
the property owners may not be willing to accept the appraised amount as the purchase price. Discussior
followed, during which several points were made: 1. Funding the appraisal provides "seed money",
without which the Federal grant application process cannot proceed. 2. The appraisal cannot be funded
by the property owner due to the potential for conflict of interest. 3. The project itself is a rare
opportunity to preserve our rapidly disappearing farmland because of the unique combination of Federal
cost share, qualifying farmland, landowner willingness, and the commitment of a land-use trust to
manage the easement. 4. Because of the nature of the farming enterprise (horse and cattle) public access
should not be a condition of approval since the objective is to preserve working farmland. 5. The owners
stated that their only motivation was the protection of the land and that they would not back out of the
project.
Considering the above, Ammy moved that the CC reaffirm its previous commitment to pay for the initial
appraisal of the conservation easement value so that the grant application can proceed. Ayn seconded
All voted in favor.
2. DeStefano/Phipps. Ammy contacted Stephen DeStefano about the family's interest in selling
properties they own adjacent to the Doherty conservation area. Stephen indicated that he is willing to
consider offers on two lots 260-48 (~60 acres) and 260-49 (~35 acres). Since these areas are forested,
they would qualify for the use of the Phipps grant funds. Ammy suggested that the CC conduct a site
visit and complete a criteria rating sheet. She will contact Stephen to obtain permission for the visit.
Conservation Lands:

suggested that members provide written comments before the next meeting to facilitate the discussion.

Re: Nadine Road Culverts and Donna Drive Culvert - Engineering Services for Design, Permitting and
Bidding
Dear Mr. Ranfos:
KV Partners is pleased to submit this proposal to provide professional engineering services for this project. We are
currently under contract to provide professional engineering services with the Town and conditions specified in
the Agreement apply to this Task Order.
We understand that the Town plans to replace deteriorated corrugated metal pipe culverts (72" and 42") on Nadine
Road and a 24" corrugated metal pipe culvert on Donna Drive. Larger culverts that comply with NHDES Stream
Crossing Rules to provide the required hydraulic capacity will be installed on Nadine Road. The watershed
associated with these culverts is about 820 acres (72") and 281 acres (42") so the stream crossing will be classified
as a Tier 3 and Tier 2 respectively crossing. The Tier 3 stream will require an open bottom box culvert and the 42"
Tier 2 stream will require a pipe with natural streambed materials inside the pipe. The Town also plans to replace
a 24" corrugated metal pipe culvert on Donna Drive with a new 24" culvert in the same location. Following is the
scope of work required to complete the design of this project:
SCOPE OF SERVICES
Task 1 - Field Survey and Base Plans
The purpose of this task is to complete an existing conditions survey and prepare base plans to complete
the design and permit documents at three locations. Specific tasks include:
• Establish NAVD88.
• Establish Horizontal NAD83.
• Obtain location, pavement, centerline, utilities, etc.
• Obtain topographic information within the project limits at one-foot contour.
• Topography to extend 150' along the road from the centerline of the road and culvert in both directions.
• Topography to extend 100' up and down stream and 100' off centerline stream in each direction.
• Locate centerline of the stream.
• Additional location on culvert bottom, side, top, to show hydraulic opening.
• Locate sewer each side of culvert and obtain invert information.
• Delineation and Location of Wetlands Flags.
• Delineation of Top of Bank and OHWM as needed.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
June 17, 2026 6:00 PM
Present: Chair Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman Peter Gagyi,
Selectwoman Sandy Goulet
Excused: Selectman Miller
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:
II.
III.
Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00 PM.
Citizens Comment
The Chair opened the meeting with an opportunity for citizens to raise matters not
listed on the agenda. No public comments were offered. The Chair then summarized
the evening's agenda, including the public hearing on engineering funds for culvert
work, the Water Department discussion on PFAS remediation, adoption of the
Economic Development Committee Rules of Procedure, town code updates,
manifests, minutes, and reports. Selectman Miller was noted absent.
No citizen comments were received at the opening of the meeting.
Scheduled Meetings
Public Hearing removal of funds from the Roadway and Infrastructure Capital
Reserve Fund
The Board held a public hearing on the proposed withdrawal of $29,900 from the
Roadway and Infrastructure Capital Reserve Fund for engineering services related to
culvert replacements on Nadine Road and Donna Drive. The Board reviewed the
summary of the KV Partners LLC proposal submitted May 15, which covered
survey and base mapping, hydrologic and hydraulic analysis, design work, wetland
permitting, final plans and specifications, bid documents, cost estimates, and bidding
assistance. The work involves two culverts on Nadine Road, identified as 72-inch
and 42-inch culverts, and one 24-inch culvert on Donna Drive.
Board members noted the matter had been discussed extensively at the prior meeting
and raised follow-up questions concerning the proposal's reference to three culvert
locations versus two locations in the fee table, whether construction oversight was
included, abutter notification, and the anticipated construction approach for the
larger structure.

It was clarified by the Public Works Director that the quoted amount covered all
three culverts, that construction oversight by KV Partners LLC would be a separate
cost, that abutters would be notified after bid award, and that the larger replacement
would be an open-bottom box culvert. The public hearing was closed at 6:05 p.m.
Proposal amount: $29,900 lump sum.
Fee breakdown reviewed: $10,700 survey, $7,000 preliminary design, and $12,200
final design.
Estimated schedule: 14 weeks from notice to proceed
Selectwoman Goulet motioned to approve the withdrawal of $29,900 from the
Roadway and Infrastructure Capital Reserve Fund for engineering work on Nadine
Road and Donna Drive, seconded by Selectman Christiansen. Motion passed 4-0.
Water Department Discussion - PEAS Remediation Update
Kevin Brasley, Chairman of the Board of Water Commissioners, provided an update
on the Water Department's PFAS remediation efforts.
He reported that there had been little substantive change since the prior year and that
Pembroke remains dependent on Concord City Council action to approve the
proposed interconnection with the Concord Water System.
Mr. Brasley stated that DES continues to press Concord to place the matter on its
agenda and that the state's preferred path remains interconnection rather than pursuit
of additional new wells.
He explained that treatment and disposal issues remain unsettled statewide, and that
while filtration technology exists, disposal of contaminated media remains a
significant cost and policy problem. Mr. Brasley reported that current state limits are
15 parts per trillion, while future limits are expected to be about 4 parts per trillion
in 2029, possibly later if implementation is delayed. Pembroke is currently below
the 15 parts per trillion limit but slightly above the future standard.
Chair Brasley also described unexplained fluctuations in sampling, including a
seven-week period last year with no detections and more recent detections in Well
106. He said the town's watering restriction remains necessary to reduce pumping
stress and limit contaminant draw into the system.
The Selectboard discussed the risks of long-term dependence on Concord, Concord's
own supply constraints, and the consequences if Pembroke cannot complete the
interconnection. Mr. Brasley stated that if town wells were ever shut down by DES,
the Bear Brook wells alone would not be sufficient to supply the system.
Chair Brasley reviewed project funding and noted that the town currently has
financing in place for the interconnection project and has received litigation and
settlement proceeds to offset future rate impacts.

IV.
V.
Old Business
None
New Business
The Board reviewed the proposed Economic Development Committee Rules of
Procedure. It was reported that Carolyn had updated the document to align it with
town code and that the Economic Development Committee had reviewed the revised
draft on June 1 and voted unanimously to forward it to the Board of Selectmen for
adoption. During discussion, the Board clarified that committee terms are generally
three years and reviewed the committee's composition as 11 total members, including
eight public members and three appointed members.
Selectwoman Goulet made a motion to approve the Economic Development
Committee Rules of Procedure as presented, seconded by Selectman Christiansen.
Motion passed 4-0.
Review of Town Code Updates - Chapters 138, 152, 154, 165, 167, and 172
The Board reviewed proposed updates to several town code chapters.
For Chapter 138, taxation language was updated to reflect the changes at Town
Meeting to elderly exemptions, veterans' exemptions, disabled veterans' exemptions,
and credits.
The Board requested a future breakdown of the number of people benefiting from
those items.
For the Board of Selectmen chapter 152, clerical and organizational revisions were
reviewed, including updates from tape-recorded meetings to video-recorded meetings
and a request to add more flexible language for off-site meetings so the recording
requirement remains workable when meetings are held away from Town Hall
The cash receipts policy chapter 154 update included raising the weekly cash
threshold from $1,500 to $3,500, noting use of a cash-counting machine if available,
and adding fraud-detection and positive-pay language. The Board also reviewed
updates concerning nonsufficient-funds checks, including certified-mail notice,
regular-mail notice, and the practice of not accepting partial payments on a bounced-
check obligation so the town may continue to proceed under the statutory process.
Chapter 165 Financial Policies, the Board indicated no change was needed to the
existing percentage targets in the fund balance policy and noted those figures were
supported by the auditors.
Chapter 167 Joint Loss Management Committee language were also reviewed
Chapter 172, relating to Parks and Recreation, was pulled for additional committee
review, and related Energy Committee review work was also referenced as still in
process.

Meeting Minutes
July 6, 2026
Attendance
Members: Sharon Morris, Chair; Jessica Stevenson, Vice Chair; Matt Miller, Selectmen
Rep.; Clint Hanson, Planning Board Rep; Chuck Schmidt; Brendan Williams
Staff: Carolyn Cronin, Town Planner
Excused: Chuck Therrien
Business
1. EDC Facebook Page Business Spotlight Posts
The Committee reviewed responses to its Facebook outreach inviting local businesses to
participate in a business spotlight feature. Businesses identified for possible inclusion were
Monroe Plumbing and Heating, Majestic Moonbeam Farm, The Creative Duckling,
Kinstruct Tiny Homes, and Shirley's Kitchen. Members discussed using a short, consistent
question set for each spotlight and favored a brief written post with a business photo rather
than video. The Committee also discussed whether featured businesses should have a tax
ID. Majestic Moonbeam Farm was noted as not yet having one, and members supported
allowing time for that to be resolved while moving ahead with other businesses. By
consensus, the Committee chose to begin with Monroe Plumbing and Heating and to
prepare a standard list of questions that can be reused for future spotlights.
The set of questions that the EDC agreed upon were:
1) Where are you from and what brought your business to Pembroke?
2) Where do your customers come from?
3) How many employees do you have?
4) What do you enjoy most about your job?
5) What piece of advice would you give someone trying to start a business?
Members agreed that a phone call or in-person conversation could be offered if that is
easier for a business owner than replying in writing. A photo of the owner and/or business
will be requested for each post.
Action items:
• C. Cronin will email the final Business Spotlight questions to the members.
• J. Stevenson will contact Monroe Plumbing and Heating.

2. Discussion of Community Organizations on Website
The EDC continued its discussion of whether the town website should include community
organizations, local resources, or business-related information. S. Morris said that a list
developed through the Friends of the Library included organizations such as Scouts and
other clubs. M. Miller reported that he had compiled categories including parks, arts and
craft studios, historical markers, food, conservation areas, retail businesses, services, the
Suncook Rod and Gun Club, and the Town Library after searching Google maps and
online sources. C. Cronin checked the Bow website and they list the athletic club, booster
club, Boy Scouts, Cub Scouts, Garden Club, Men's Club, and Rotary.
Members noted that information about Pembroke amenities is scattered and difficult to
locate. C. Cronin reviewed the town's prior experience with website business listings
becoming outdated when businesses closed, moved, or changed contact information. The
EDC had previously built an internal business list using New Hampshire Secretary of State
data, and chose not to publish it because of maintenance and privacy concerns.
The Committee agreed to defer a final website recommendation until the broader town
website project advances, and to work on a written concept for the Select Board describing
possible categories and a maintenance approach. Members discussed beginning with civic
and community organizations before considering any business listings. The EDC agreed
that permission should be obtained before listing organizations or groups on the website. A
maintenance plan and periodic verification were identified as essential if any listing system
is created on the website.
Action items:
•
M. Miller will email his compiled list to the EDC members.
• The next step is for the EDC to prepare a written proposal for the Select Board
outlining possible categories and how information would be maintained.
3. Bike Rack in Village
The Committee revisited the proposal for a bicycle rack in the village. C. Cronin
summarized prior review of the item and noted that Public Works had previously identified
a landscape island in the parking lot as its preferred location because a sidewalk location
would interfere with winter plowing and ADA access. C. Cronin explained that a resident
had concerns about the location being too secluded and not wanting to park expensive
bikes there. Therefore, the proposal never progressed.
The EDC discussed an alternate location at the small state right-of-way or easement near
Main Street and Glass Street, where there is historical signage, a flagpole, and a cannon.
Several members felt that site would be more visible to cyclists and closer to village
businesses. Discussion included earlier involvement by the American Legion or VFW,
current local maintenance of the area, and ongoing work by Meet Me in Suncook on a
replacement flag and lighting. The Committee agreed that the immediate next step is to
determine the state approval process before taking formal action on a location. No formal
decision was made at the meeting. They will pursue gathering information at this point.

This topic was discussed at the previous meeting. The EDC discussed ideas for a
Pembroke bike tour intended to encourage cyclists to use local roads in lieu of the rail trail,

White Sands, Memorial Park, the community garden near the Congregational Church,

conservation land. Members also noted that local food stops and the planned ice cream
stand could help attract riders to stop in the village. The concept is intended as an
informational guide rather than a formally designated trail. The Committee agreed to
continue the bike tour concept using an informal mapping approach.

PEMBROKE CEMETERY COMMISSION
July 9, 2026
Minutes
Present: James Garvin, Ellen Paulsen (chair), Victor J. Ranfos (Superintendent of Cemeteries), Zachary
Sawyer, Fleda Young.
1. Chair Ellen Paulsen called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m.
2. On a motion by Fleda Young, seconded by Zachary Sawyer, the minutes of the meeting of June
11, 2026, were approved as submitted.
New business:
3. By a letter dated June 21, 2026, Jane Bates, holder with her husband of burial licenses for Lots
49 A&B in Section 5 of Evergreen Cemetery, requested that the Town of Pembroke repurchase
Lot 49 B because the family no longer has a need for this lot. By unanimous agreement, the
Commission voted to recommend to the Board of Selectmen that the town repurchase Lot 49 B.
The Bates family purchased Lots 49 A&B for $700, the price for two lots, in August 2018. Since
the price for a burial permit for a single lot is $400 and Mr. and Mrs. Bates intend to retain the
permit for Lot 49 A, the Commission will recommend to the Board of Selectmen that the town
offer to repurchase Lot 49 B for the balance of $300, leaving the Bates family in possession of
the license for Lot 49 A. Secretary Garvin will convey this recommendation to the Board of
Selectmen.
4. The Commission discussed the ownership of the French Cemetery on North Pembroke Road.
Earlier research had disclosed that the town assessor's card, prepared by AxisGIS, the contracted
appraiser, indicates that the cemetery is the property of the Town of Pembroke. This is confirmed
by the town tax map (Map ID #2508-00CM-009), which shows that the cemetery, labeled as
"CEM 9," as a town-owned land parcel separate from the adjacent land of the French family.
Zachary Sawyer reported that he had heard that the town had assumed ownership of the formerly
private cemetery during the 1950s. The Commission agreed to assess the current condition and
potential needs of the French Cemetery and to plan to address its care from this time onward.
5. The Commission discussed the guidance for the cleaning and care of gravestones provided by
New Hampshire statutes, which Zachary Sawyer had previously researched and sent to
Commission members. With further study and discussion, the Commission will plan to add
language derived from these statutes to Chapter 155 ("Cemeteries") of the Pembroke Town Code
and make note of the language of the statutes in our next Annual Report for the Pembroke Town
Report for 2027.

2
Old business:
6. Chair Ellen Paulsen reported that she had submitted funding request to the Capital Improvement
Program (CIP) Committee through Town Administrator David Jodoin. Public Works Director V.
J. Ranfos noted that it should not be necessary for Chair Paulsen to attend the upcoming meeting
of the CIP Committee to discuss the request.
7. V. J. Ranfos noted that he had received an inquiry regarding the proposed establishment of a
"scattering garden" for cremation ashes in Buck Street Cemetery. This prompted V. J. to urge that
the Commission move forward with the establishment of such an amenity. We will add the
project to our Six Year Cemetery Plan and will probably begin to add funding for the necessary
landscaping to future CIP Committee proposals, possibly making use of some of the stored
granite that was salvaged from the former front wall of Evergreen Cemetery.
8. Relating to this subject, Secretary Garvin added that he has begun to research the rumored
establishment of a "cremation garden" by the Town of Hooksett. He has learned that the
regulations of the Hooksett Cemetery Commission require that "cremains shall be interred in a
container." At the same time, the Hooksett town website describes Fraser Memorial Park on K
Avenue, which is in a residential neighborhood and is not listed as a Hooksett municipal
cemetery, as a facility that offers grave sites and "cremation gardens." Garvin has left an inquiry
and a request for clarification with the chair of the Hooksett Cemetery Commission and will
report future findings to the Commission.
9. Zachary Sawyer reported that he has been in contact with Nicholas Allan from Celebrate Life
Company. Zachary distributed links to videos that describe the services of the company,
including a quick demonstration video, a video demonstrating the company's administrative
software, and an example of a client's cemetery map. Mr. Allan offered to provide quotes for
services relating to Pembroke cemeteries, noting that some associated fees include an
"onboarding fee" that depends on the size and complexity of the cemetery and an annual service
fee of $1,000 per year. The Commission agreed that we should add cemetery mapping to our Six
Year Cemetery Plan and should consider seeking funding through the CIP Committee but should
not move too far forward without the approval of the Board of Selectmen and relevant town staff.
10. The next regular meeting of the Pembroke Cemetery Commission will be at 6:00 p.m. on
Thursday, August 13 at the Public Works Department headquarters on Exchange Street in
Suncook Village.
11. There being no further business, the meeting was adjourned at 6:50 p.m.
Respectfully submitted.
James L. Garvin, Secretary

Summary: Electricity Supply Contract Renewal - Constellation Energy
Prepared for the Pembroke Select Board - July 15, 2026
BACKGROUND
• Quotes were received through Energy Professionals (the Town's power broker) from 5 different electricity
suppliers for term lengths ranging from 1 to 5 years.
- Pembroke has used Energy Professionals as its broker in the past, including for the current contract with
Constellation Energy, which expires in November 2026 (existing rate: 8.22 ¢/kWh, on a 48-month term).
RECOMMENDATION
• Rates have increased since the previous contract for a variety of market reasons. After evaluating the
available options through Energy Professionals, the Energy Committee recommends extending the Town's
current agreement with Constellation Energy for a new 5-year term.
- This is generally a favorable time of year to shop for a new contract, as supply is plentiful and rates are
relatively low compared to winter, when supply rates typically rise.
- The quoted supply rate is 10.510 c/kWh, but this quote is only valid for 24 hours; the rate at signing may
differ slightly. Once approved, Energy Professionals will confirm the rate is close to what the Select Board
approved, and the Committee will flag any significant deviation.
- The newly implemented Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Initiative (DASI) charge from ISO New England adds
some uncertainty, since it is currently an estimate; the final supply rate will be adjusted to reflect any change
to the DASI charge.
- All quotes received on June 10th are attached for the Board's review.
WHY EXTEND WITH CONSTELLATION
• Constellation is the Town's current supplier, making an extension straightforward.
• The renewal agreement has been reviewed by Town legal counsel and Primex (the Town's insurance
carrier), who recommended minor language changes. Those changes are currently under review by
Constellation Energy as of July 7th.
• Constellation offers several features that are attractive relative to other suppliers:
- 100% Swing: Honors the contracted supply rate even if Pembroke's actual usage exceeds forecast, reducing
risk to the Town. Not all suppliers offer this.
- Blend and Extend: Allows the Town to renegotiate its fixed-rate plan by extending the contract term,
immediately blending the existing (higher) contract rate with the lower current market rate - locking in
savings without waiting for the current agreement to expire. Other suppliers attach more contingencies to
• For reference, savings for the town through our current Constellation Energy supply contract are over
$5,000 for the past 12-month period compared to the default Eversource utility supply rate (details on
second page)
The Energy Committee recommends the Select Board approve a 5-year extension of the Town's supply
agreement with Constellation Energy and welcomes any questions.

BOARD OF SELECTMEN
TOWN OF PEMBROKE, NH
July 15, 2026 6:00 PM
Present: Chair Karen Yeaton, Selectman Bryan Christiansen, Selectman Peter Gagyi, Selectman
Matt Miller
Excused: Selectwoman Goulet
Staff: Town Administrator David Jodoin
Call to Order:

Chairman Yeaton called the meeting to order at 6:00 PM.
Citizens Comment
Scheduled Meetings
Public Hearing Town Code Updates Chapter 138, 152, 154, 165, 167
The Board opened the public hearing at 6:03 PM to consider updates to Chapters 138,
132, 134, 163, and 16/ ot the Town Code. The Chair reviewed that Chapter 138
reflected taxation changes for disability and elderly exemptions previously approved
at Town Meeting; Chapter 152 updated Selectmen bylaws, including committee
representation and recording of meetings; and Chapters 154, 165, and 167 contained
housekeeping updates to cash receipts, financial policies, and the Joint Loss
Management Committee.
During the discussion, David noted that additional revisions to the solid waste chapter
remained under separate review with Gerry Fleury and would be brought forward
later.
No public comment was offered, and the hearing was closed at 6:04 PM. Motion by
Selectman Christiansen, seconded by Selectman Miller to accept the updates as
presented. Motion passed 4-0.
Old Business
Stage/Roof
At the request of the Chair and without objection, the Board took up the stage/roof
update out of agenda order so the attendees present for that item could be heard.
Mark Chevrette, representing Old Home Day and also Public Works, and Dana
Carlucci of the Building Committee reviewed the status of the replacement stage
plans. Dana Carlucci reported that the plans had been distributed, including to Tom

Hebert, and that the current design is for a 16-by-24 structure consisting of beams and
roof only, requiring either a concrete slab or a deck.
Discussion focused on whether to relocate the stage rather than reuse the existing site,
where concerns were raised about uneven ground, wetlands, and the stability of the
existing supports.
Dana Carlucci stated that prior discussions had favored reorienting the stage north-
south facing the basketball courts to reduce the effect of the westerly sun and improve
viewing from the pavilion area near Rose's building. He also noted that Sean Benoit,
who had previously offered to help with the slab, had since died.
Dana advised that available capital funding appeared sufficient for a new slab and
installation, but that delay would likely increase cost as lumber prices rise.
David explained that there would be a joint discussion with the Recreation
Commission members and the Building Committee members on July 30 after the CIP
meeting, and that discussion should come back to the Board for a final decision on
how to proceed at the August 5 meeting.
Energy Committee - Discussion on electric rate renewal
Rich Wengenroth of the Energy Committee presented a recommendation on renewal
of the Town's municipal electricity supply contract, which expires in November 2026.
Rich reported that the Town's broker, Energy Professionals, had obtained updated
market pricing and that Constellation Energy remained the lowest-cost supplier under
consideration. The Energy Committee recommended a 60-month term.
Rich stated that the updated five-year Constellation quote was 10.677 cents per
kilowatt-hour, compared with an earlier quote of 10.51 cents, and noted that current

1. SERVICE REQUESTS FOR 2027

2. SERVICE DESCRIPTION
1) Pembroke Emergency Medical Service (hereafter "Pembroke EMS" or "PEMS") is the municipal ambulance
service for the Town of Pembroke.
2) Pembroke EMS staffs one (1) ambulance, with at least one (1) Paramedic and one (1) other
EMS Provider. The other EMS Provider may be an EMT, Advanced EMT or another Paramedic.
The ambulance is staffed 24/7 and is housed at the Pembroke Public Safety Center.
3) Pembroke EMS responds to approximately 650 to 700 runs per year in the Town of Pembroke and
about 200 runs per year to other communities. This gives the Service an annual call volume of
850-900 runs per year.
3. PEMBROKE EMS CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT PLAN (CIP) SUMMARY:
1) Pembroke EMS' CIP is based upon a 12-year replacement cycle for all equipment and
ambulances.
2) When an ambulance is purchased or replaced, all equipment within the ambulance will
also be replaced. This will include the stretcher, stair chair, cardiac monitor, ventilator,
CPR device, and medication pumps.
3) New ambulances shall be the "Primary" ambulance for six (6) years and will be used on the
majority of the EMS calls responded to by Pembroke EMS during this period. The unit
designator for the primary ambulance in Pembroke shall be "Ambulance 8". This unit designator
is unique in the region and was selected to minimize any confusion over the radio.
4) The second ambulance or rather the older one, shall be held in reserve or back-up for
Pembroke EMS. This ambulance shall be used when the primary ambulance is not available
while maintenance conerns are being addressed OR when it can be staffed by additional
members of Pembroke EMS and qualified members of the Pembroke Fire Department to respond
to 2nd EMS calls. The unit designator for this ambulance shall be "Ambulance 9"
6) Pembroke EMS' CIP projects the anticipated capital expenditures for the total replacement
cycle of all vehicles and equipment using a 5% annual increase in costs.
4. DESCRIPTION OF VEHICLES & EQUIPMENT
1) AMBULANCES: Pembroke EMS shall maintain two (2) ambulances; a primary ambulance and
a reserve ambulance. It is estimated that the Service will respond to approximately 850-900

incidents each year.
Pembroke EMS has created ambulance specifications to ensure our EMS providers have adequate space in
the patient compartment when multiple EMS providers are required to meet the medical needs of our critical
patients. These specifications are also intended to create the safest possible environment for our staff and
patients. The Service uses and intends to continue, to utilize a Ford F-550 4x4 diesel chassis (or complarable
chassis by other manufacturers) for its weight capacity, capabilities and handling.
2) POWER-LOAD SYSTEM: This item is typically part of the ambulance specifications and
allows for the safe loading and unloading of patients within the ambulance by removing all
lifting by EMS providers during this evolution. This decreases the risk of back and extremity
injury for the Service's staff as well as decreased the possibility of patient's being dropped and
injured. Finally, the power-load is a positive, multi-point stretcher securing device. In the
event the ambulance is in a collision and rolls over, the stretcher, with the patient, will remain
locked in place removing the possibility of the stretcher dislodging and further injuring the
patient or causing serious injury to the EMS provider. The power-load is serviced each year by
STRYKER as part of the service agreement.
3) STRETCHERS: Pembroke EMS uses a STRYKER PowerPRO XPS and Power PRO 2 stretchers. This
stretcher has proven to be reliable in the pre-hospital setting and being a mechanical
stretcher, removes the need for EMS staff to lift the patient once they are on the stretcher. The
stretchers are maintained each year by STRYKER as part of the service agreement.
4) STAIR CHAIR: A stair chair is used to remove and carry a person out of their residence in a
seated position. On the 2017 ambulance, there is a STRYKER StairPRO stair chair. The 2025
ambulance has a STRYKER XPEDITION powered stair chair. As with the powered stretchers, the new
stair chair further decreases lifting for the EMS crew while they are moving a patient up or down stairs.
This new device only requires the crew to balance the stair chair during this evolution. Both stair
chairs are maintained each year by STRYKER as part of the service agreement
5) CARDIAC MONITOR: Cardiac monitors are used by advanced providers to monitor a
person's heart rhythm, obtain electro-cardiograms (ECG's), obtain blood pressures, measure
oxygen levels, monitor exhaled carbon dioxide, detects carbon monoxide, defibrilate, used as an AED,
cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing and documenting times of treatments rendered
The 2017 ambulance (Back -up) utilizes a Life Pak 15v4 that was purchased in 2024. The 2025
ambulance is equipped with the Life Pak 35.
The Life Pak 35 provides all the same treatment capabilities as the Life Pak 15. The LP35 is lighter,
utilizes touchscreen technology for ease of use and presents patient data in a formate that is easier
to see and interpret.
6) MECHANICAL CPR DEVICE: Pembroke EMS uses the LUCAS III CPR Device by STRYKER. These
devices are widely used within the region. The LUCAS Ill allows for uninterupted CPR to a
person in cardiac arrest. This frees up EMS providers to perform other treatments while
maintaining a continuous blood flow to vital organs (particularly the brain). Each ambulance has
a LUCAS III CPR device as part of its equipment.
7) VENTILATOR: The Service uses a Zoll Z-Vent Ventilator. This device allows for the mechanical
ventilation of those patients who are not breathing on their own after an advanced airway has been
placed. The ventilator also allows the Service's paramedics to perform CPAP and BiPAP. These
treatments are intended to support a patient's breathing efforts with the goal of improving their
respiratory status and to avoid the need of being intubated and placed on a ventilator. This device
is maintained by Zoll annually as part of a service agreements.
8) MEDICATION INFUSION PUMPS: The Service has two (2) infusion pumps on each ambulance.
nfusion pumps are used to administer certain intravenous medications over a specified period o
ime. Typically, infusion medications are used in the most critical patients or when a specific volume
of fluids are to be administered to a pediatric patient. Pembroke EMS purchased four (4) infusion
pumps in 2025 to replace the older pumps the were used prior.

Public Hearing - 2027 CIP Requests
Rosemarie Michaud opened the public hearing on the 2021 CIP requests at 6:05 p.m. Rosemarie called to
ublic comment and questions. There were no members of the public so Rosemarie closed the public hearing a
6:06 p.m.
David Jodoin reported that the Energy Committee had reviewed the Library solar proposal and available
incentives and tax credits would require the project to be live, witnessed, and producing by December 31, 2027.
Members discussed questions raised at a prior Select Board meeting, including Select Board Miller's statement
that the estimates were intended as turnkey figures, while also noting remaining questions about structural
review, warranties, interconnection studies, utility upgrades, and any necessary roof reinforcement.

David advised that a structural analysis would be required for the Library roof and also he had a concern on the
Fire side of the Safety Center, while the Police side was not expected to have the same issue.
He further stated that potential savings in the camera project originally developed by Police Chief Gaskell and
now being refined with Fire Chief Paulson for Town Hall, Public Works, Police, Fire, and EMS could leave
additional money available in the Town Facilities and Grounds Capital Reserve Fund.
Members discussed the Library's electric costs, which were estimated at approximately $1,000 per month, and
noted one estimate showing an 8 to 9 year payback period
Ranking of 2027 CIP Requests - Town Facilities and Grounds/Library Solar
Town Facilities and Grounds Capital Reserve Fund Deposit
The first item that the committee reviewed was the proposal to deposit $175,000 into the Town Facilities and
Grounds Capital Reserve Fund.
Rosemarie Michaud asked if these requests could be reduced. David stated the deposit schedule was designed to
support future Town Hall, Library, Safety Center, and related town building needs.
The committee voted as follows on the deposit request. High priority - 2, Medium - 2, and Low -1.
The committee then discussed the proposed Library solar project at an estimated costs of $150,000, exclusive of
any later structural engineering or roof-related work that might be required after further review.
In discussing future building needs, David stated that the current reserve schedule was intended to support the
planned 2029 Safety Center roof and potential solar work, subject to later revision by the Select Board, the
Budget Committee, and Town Meeting.
The committee voted as follows: High priority - 3; Medium - 2
Town Clock Capital Reserve Fund Deposit
The committee reviewed the request for $3,000 to be deposited into the Town Clock Capital Reserve Fund as
well as the next proposed expense in 2032.
Gene Gauss asked what the prior repair costs were. David explained that it was around $35,000 and the money
came out of surplus to pay for it.
The committee voted as follows: High priority - 2; Low - 3
Property Revaluation/Update Capital Reserve Fund Deposit
The committee reviewed the request for $30,000 to be deposited into the Property Revaluation/Update Capital
Reserve Fund.
David explained the current situation in Town where the homes are still selling for much more than we have
them assessed at. If the trend continues commercial property will in effect be paying a higher burden of taxes.

The Board is discussing the possibility of adjusting the values in 2027 to get back in line. Currently the Town's
ratio is at 83% and when we did the revaluation we were at 95%.
Michael Rodney questioned whether the committee even needed to vote on this.
David explained that in the past the same comment had come up and the Chair at the time requested a vote.
The Board voted as follows: High priority - 2; Medium - 1; Low - 2
Statistical Update
Request to withdraw $75,000 from the Property Revaluation Fund
The committee voted High priority - 1; Low - 4
Cemetery Capital Reserve Fund Expense
David explained that there was no need to put any money in the fund this year because they still had enough to
do the proposed work. He also commented that he would like to see the Commission go out at least 10-15 years
with a plan of necessary expenses.
The committee discussed the Cemetery request of $6,000 to repair grave markers.
Rosemarie Michaud commented that some of the expense for the grave marker repairs may also come out of
perpetual care and that would lower the costs.
The committee voted High priority - 5.
Major Fire Equipment Capital Reserve Fund Deposit
The 2027 request was to deposit into the Fund $250,000
The committee reviewed the Fire Department capital schedule and emphasized the importance of maintaining
long-range reserve funding because of sharp increases in apparatus and equipment costs.
Gene Gauss commented that a heavy rescue unit that had cost approximately $169,000 in 1999 would now be in
the range of $1.2 million.
The entire committee voted High priority -5.
David explained that the current CIP plan that the Town uses is one of the best that he has seen over the years,
whether it be as an Auditor or a municipal employee. The Town's Treasurer also hands this out to other
communities as a plan.
He also commented that you can go one Town North or South and you can see what happens when you do not
stick to a plan.
